heroLead: Almost all of the land under and around Oljato-Monument Valley sits inside the Navajo Nation, which changes the entire mineral-ownership picture compared to the rest of San Juan County.
intro: We want to be direct about this one before anything else: the great majority of mineral acreage at Monument Valley is either tribal trust land or individual Indian allotment land held by the Navajo Nation and its members, managed through the Bureau of Indian Affairs, not the county recorder. We do not buy tribal trust minerals and we are not positioned to navigate BIA approval processes for allotted interests, and we say so plainly rather than stringing an owner along.

Where we can help is the smaller set of privately held, fee-simple mineral interests that sit outside the reservation boundary but still carry a Monument Valley or Oljato address, often old grazing or homestead parcels near the highway corridor toward Mexican Hat.

sections.heading: Fee mineral acreage versus tribal trust land
paragraphs: If your ownership traces back to a BIA allotment number or a tribal assignment, that interest is governed by federal Indian land law and typically requires Secretary of the Interior approval to convey, a process we don't participate in. If instead you hold a deed recorded at the San Juan County recorder's office in Monticello, tracing to a fee patent rather than an allotment, that's a fee mineral interest we can evaluate like any other in the county.
The fastest way to sort this out is to send us whatever paperwork you have. We can usually tell within a day which category an interest falls into.

sections.heading: Paradox Basin geology near the reservation edge
paragraphs: This corner of San Juan County sits at the southern edge of the Paradox Basin, where historic production came from the Mississippian-age Aneth field to the east and scattered Permian and Pennsylvanian objectives closer to the Arizona line. It's a mature, slower-moving part of the play compared to the Cane Creek trend up near Moab, with most activity being workovers and secondary recovery on legacy units rather than new exploration.
For fee owners here, that maturity actually helps with valuation, because decades of production history give us real decline curves to price against instead of speculation.

sections.heading: What to send if you think your interest is fee land
paragraphs: A recorded deed or patent number, a legal description, and any royalty statements you've received are the starting point. If your family has documentation showing the interest was patented rather than allotted, that resolves the question quickly.

We'll tell you honestly if what you have turns out to be tribal trust or allotted land, and point you toward the BIA Southern Ute or Navajo agency for guidance rather than pursue a purchase we can't complete.

faqs.question: Can you buy my Navajo Nation allotment mineral interest?
faqs.answer: No. Allotted and tribal trust minerals require Bureau of Indian Affairs approval to transfer and we don't participate in that process. We only purchase fee mineral interests recorded with San Juan County.

faqs.question: How do I know if my interest is fee land or an allotment?
faqs.answer: Check your deed or patent paperwork. A BIA allotment number or reference to trust status means it's not something we can buy; a standard recorded deed with a legal description usually means fee land.

faqs.question: Is there active drilling near Monument Valley right now?
faqs.answer: Most current activity is workovers and secondary recovery on long-established Aneth-area units rather than new wells, which is typical for this mature stretch of the Paradox Basin.
